title: Your first 30/60/90 days
summary: Turn your new AI role into a clear plan: learn fast in 30 days, contribute by 60, and own work by 90.
objectives: Build a 30/60/90 day plan with concrete, measurable goals
Spend your first 30 days learning the codebase, data and people
Ship a small, safe win early to build trust
Ask good questions and document what you learn
Set up your tools, environment and access on day one
Use feedback loops and one-on-ones to course-correct
Avoid common new-starter mistakes in AI and data teams

quiz.q: What is the main goal of your first 30 days?
options: Learn the systems, data and people
quiz.why: The first month is for learning — the code, the data, the workflows and who does what — before making big changes.

quiz.q: What kind of first contribution is best in week two or three?
quiz.why: A small, well-scoped, reviewed change (a bug fix or doc) builds trust and teaches the workflow without much risk.

quiz.q: Why keep a running document of questions and answers as you onboard?
quiz.answer: It speeds up your own learning, captures gaps in the docs, and helps the next new starter.
quiz.why: Writing things down turns scattered Slack answers into a reusable resource and shows you are organised.

quiz.q: What is a sensible day-one priority?
options: Get access, environment and tools working
quiz.why: Without access, a working dev environment and the right tools, you cannot learn or contribute — sort these first.

quiz.q: In your own words, what should change between the 60 and 90 day marks?
quiz.answer: You move from contributing on guided tasks to owning a feature or area more independently.
quiz.why: By 90 days you should need less hand-holding and be trusted to drive a piece of work end to end.

quiz.q: True or false — you should make major changes to models in production in your first week.
quiz.why: False. Production model changes are high-risk; learn the system, tests and review process first.

body_markdown:
## Why a 30/60/90 plan?

Starting a new AI or data job is exciting and a little overwhelming. A **30/60/90 day plan** turns that fog into three clear phases: in your first 30 days you **learn**, by 60 days you **contribute**, and by 90 days you **own** a piece of work. Writing it down — even one page — shows your manager you are intentional, and gives you something to review in your one-on-ones.

You do not need to know everything on day one. You need a direction.

## Days 0-30: Learn and set up

The first month is about absorbing, not impressing. Get your access and environment working, read the code, explore the data, and meet people. Clone the main repo and get it running locally before anything else.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-org/main-service.git
cd main-service
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pytest -q                   # confirm the tests pass
```

Keep a running document of every question you ask and the answer you get. It captures gaps in the docs and helps the next new starter.

## Days 31-60: Contribute

Now start shipping small, safe wins: a bug fix, a test, a documentation update, or a tiny feature. Get it reviewed and follow the team's workflow exactly. This is also when you might write your first real code against your stack — for example, calling the model API the team uses.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()   # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise this ticket in one line."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

Never hard-code secrets — keep your key in an environment variable like `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.

## Days 61-90: Own a piece

By now you should need less hand-holding. Take ownership of a feature, a dataset, or a small service end to end — design, build, test, ship, monitor. Ask for feedback explicitly: *what should I do more of, and what should I change?*

## Common mistakes to avoid

Don't try to rewrite everything in week one. Don't go silent when stuck for hours — ask after a sensible attempt. Don't skip the boring docs and onboarding meetings. And don't make risky production changes before you understand the tests and review process.

## Your task

Draft a one-page 30/60/90 plan for a role you are applying to, with two or three concrete goals per phase.

slides.title: Your first 30/60/90 days
slides.narration: Congratulations — you've reached the final lesson of the course, which means you're nearly ready for the job itself. In this lesson we'll plan your first ninety days in a new A I role. By the end you'll have a clear thirty, sixty, ninety day plan: learn first, contribute next, and own your work by the end.

slides.title: Why a 30/60/90 plan?
bullets: Splits onboarding into three clear phases.
30 = learn, 60 = contribute, 90 = own.
Shows your manager you are intentional.
One page is enough to start.
slides.narration: Starting a new job can feel overwhelming, so we break it into three phases. In your first thirty days you learn. By sixty days you contribute. By ninety days you own a piece of work. Writing this down on a single page shows your manager you're thoughtful, and gives you something to review together in your one-on-ones.

slides.title: Day one priorities
bullets: Get access, accounts and permissions sorted.
Set up a working dev environment.
Meet your team and manager.
Find out where the docs live.
slides.narration: On day one, don't try to impress anyone. Just get the basics working. Sort out your access and accounts, get a development environment running, and meet the people you'll work with. The single biggest blocker for new starters is access that isn't set up, so chase that early and politely.

slides.title: Days 0 to 30: learn
bullets: Read the code and run it locally.
Explore the data and pipelines.
Keep a running list of questions.
Don't make big changes yet.
slides.code:
git clone <repo-url>
cd main-service
python -m venv .venv
pip install -r requirements.txt
pytest -q
slides.narration: Your first month is for absorbing, not changing. Clone the main repository, get it running on your machine, and confirm the tests pass. Explore the data and the pipelines. And crucially, keep a running document of every question you ask and the answer you get. It captures gaps in the docs and helps the next new starter.

slides.title: Ask good questions
bullets: Try for a sensible time, then ask.
Show what you already tried.
Write the answer down for next time.
No question in week one is silly.
slides.narration: Asking questions well is a real skill. Don't go silent for hours when you're stuck, but don't fire off questions before trying either. Have a genuine go, then ask, and show what you already attempted. Always write the answer down. In your first weeks, no question is a silly question.

slides.title: Days 31 to 60: contribute
bullets: Ship small, safe, visible wins.
A bug fix, a test, or a doc update.
Get every change reviewed.
Follow the team workflow exactly.
slides.narration: In your second month, start contributing. Pick small, safe, visible wins — a bug fix, a missing test, a documentation update. Get every change reviewed and follow the team's workflow exactly, even if it feels slow. These early wins build trust and teach you how the team actually works.

slides.title: Your first AI code
bullets: Call the model API your team uses.
Keep your key in an environment variable.
Start small and get it reviewed.
slides.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
        "content": "Summarise this ticket."}])
print(msg.content[0].text)
slides.narration: Around this point you might write your first real A I code on the job. Here we call the Claude messages A P I using the anthropic library. Notice we never hard-code the secret key — the client reads it from an environment variable called ANTHROPIC underscore A P I underscore KEY. Start small, get it reviewed, and learn the team's patterns.

slides.title: Days 61 to 90: own
bullets: Take a feature or area end to end.
Design, build, test, ship, monitor.
Need less hand-holding now.
Ask for explicit feedback.
slides.narration: By your third month you should need less hand-holding. Take ownership of something end to end — a feature, a dataset, or a small service. Design it, build it, test it, ship it, and watch how it behaves. And ask for feedback directly: what should I do more of, and what should I change?

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Trying to rewrite everything week one.
Going silent when stuck for hours.
Skipping docs and onboarding meetings.
Risky production changes too early.
slides.narration: Let's flag the traps that catch new starters. Don't try to rewrite everything in week one. Don't go silent when you're stuck for hours. Don't skip the boring docs and onboarding meetings. And don't make risky production changes before you understand the tests and the review process. Patience here pays off.
